question_details.title: Will the FTC's proposed ban on non-compete agreements for most workers be enacted in more or less its current form before 2026?
question_details.description:
This question is synced with an identical question on Metaculus. The original question opened on 2025-01-01 09:31:03 and can be found [here](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/31227). This question will resolve to the same value as the synced question. The original question's background info at this time is below. 

In April 2024, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) issued a [final rule](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/04/ftc-announces-rule-banning-noncompetes) banning most non-compete agreements in the United States, claiming that this would generate over 8,500 new businesses each year, raise worker wages, lower health care costs, and boost innovation. The rule would prohibit employers from entering into or enforcing non-compete clauses with workers, including employees and independent contractors, with limited exceptions for senior executives. Employers would be required to rescind existing non-compete agreements and notify affected workers that such clauses are no longer in effect.

The rule was scheduled to take effect on September 4, 2024, however, on August 20, 2024, Judge Ada Brown of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas [blocked the rule](https://hrdailyadvisor.blr.com/2024/10/11/after-judge-blocks-ftcs-worker-non-compete-ban-now-what/) nationwide, ruling that the FTC lacked the statutory authority to implement such a ban and that the rule was "arbitrary and capricious". On October 18, 2024, the FTC [filed an appeal](https://www.psca.org/news/psca-news/2024/10/where-does-the-ftcs-non-compete-ban-stand-now/) with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

question_details.resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as **Yes** if FTC's [ban on noncompetes](https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/rules/noncompete-rule) is enacted before January 1, 2026 with at most minor changes.

As of December 2024, the current form of the regulation would apply to all workers at companies which are under FTC's jurisdiction, with a single exception of individuals earning more than $151,164 who are in a "policy-making position". It also applies to both existing and future non-compete agreements.

Minor changes are defined as amendments in the current exceptions that affect less than 10% of workers under FTC's jurisdiction (as judged by Metaculus), as changes to the notice requirements employers should give to their employees, or other changes of a similar scope as judged by Metaculus admins.

If the rule is not enacted before January 1, 2026 or if it is enacted with other changes, including but not limited to changes that affect at least 10% of workers or changes to if the rule would be applied to existing contracts at all, would resolve this question as **No**.

**FTC Walks Away From Rulemaking -- But Not The Fight On Non-Competes**
On September 5, 2025, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) shifted its strategy on non‑compete agreements by voting 3‑1 to abandon the Non‑Compete Clause Rule, a regulation that had banned most non‑compete clauses nationwide. The decision followed the FTC’s voluntary dismissal of appeals in two lawsuits—Ryan, LLC v. FTC (5th Cir.) and Properties of the Villages, Inc. v. FTC (11th Cir.)—which had issued nationwide injunctions against the Rule. Commissioner Holyoak and Chairman Ferguson stated that the Rule was "patently obvious" illegal, arguing that the FTC lacked authority to preempt state law and that it would "render categorically unlawful a species of contract that has been lawful since the eighteenth century." Ferguson also warned that the FTC would continue to enforce antitrust laws against non‑compete agreements on a case‑by‑case basis under Section 5 of the FTC Act.

Commissioner Meador concurred, calling the Rule overbroad and noting that economic considerations require a balanced approach. Commissioner Slaughter dissented, citing potential harms such as barriers to worker mobility, wage suppression, and stifled innovation, and urged the FTC to follow the Administrative Procedure Act’s notice‑and‑comment process before withdrawing the Rule.

The Rule had been promulgated on April 23, 2024 after a January 5, 2023 notice‑and‑comment period. It applied prospectively and retrospectively, preempting state non‑compete laws except those more restrictive. The Rule was originally adopted by a 3‑2 party‑line vote and was scheduled to take effect in September 2024, but was stayed by injunctions in the Ryan and Properties cases. The Ryan Court’s August 20, 2024 ruling set the Rule aside nationwide, finding it violated the APA because the FTC lacked statutory authority and the Rule was arbitrary and capricious.

Despite the Rule’s repeal, the FTC remains focused on non‑compete enforcement. Chairman Ferguson has directed a Joint Labor Task Force and issued a Request for Information to assess the scope and effects of non‑compete agreements. In September 2025, the FTC sent letters to large healthcare employers urging them to eliminate unfair or anticompetitive non‑competes, especially in rural areas. The agency also targeted Gateway Services, Inc., the largest pet cremation business, for broad non‑compete agreements that allegedly stifled job mobility and competition. The proposed consent order would require Gateway to stop enforcing existing non‑competes and prohibit future agreements.

Overall, the FTC’s strategy has moved from a blanket ban to a more tailored, case‑by‑case enforcement approach, while continuing to monitor and address non‑compete agreements that may harm competition and workers.

**Saiz to Facilitate Partial Retirement in the Administration with Interim Staff**
The Spanish government is studying the opening of a transitional period that would allow temporary staff to act as releasers, thereby unblocking the backlog of partial‑retirement requests for public‑sector labour personnel. The Ministry of Social Security is finalising a formula to reverse the block caused by the new partial‑retirement regime that entered into force on 1 April. The last tripartite pension agreement, reached a little over a year ago, introduced changes that did not consider the impact on public‑sector labour staff. The new rule requires that a releaser be hired permanently, full‑time, and remain employed for at least two years after the partial‑retirement process ends. This rigidity has made it difficult for administrations to create fixed positions, leading to a backlog that previously could be resolved by hiring temporary staff. According to the article, there were about 250,000 labour contracts in the administration in 2024, and the total public workforce was 3.5 million, of which 981,000 were temporary, giving a temporary rate of almost 28 %. The EU Court of Justice, in a 13 June 2024 ruling, declared that successive temporary contracts in the public sector constitute abuse and urged administrations to convert them to permanent contracts or provide deterrent compensation. The Supreme Court has submitted a question to the Court of Justice about the procedure for long‑duration interim staff, which could clarify the application of the ruling. The Ministry says it will wait for an agreement with social partners before finalising the solution, but sources say the plan is to keep the old rule for a transitional period until public administrations can fill the positions with permanent staff. All forecasting experts unanimously assess the probability that the FTC's proposed ban on non-compete agreements for most workers will be enacted in more or less its current form before 2026 as essentially zero or close to zero. The consensus is grounded in several decisive factors: 

1. The rule was vacated nationwide by federal courts on grounds that the FTC lacked statutory authority, citing the 'major questions doctrine' and labeling the rule 'arbitrary and capricious.' 
2. The FTC, under new Trump-appointed leadership, has voluntarily dismissed all legal appeals and publicly abandoned the rulemaking, with a commission vote confirming the withdrawal.
3. The Trump administration and new FTC chair have clearly shifted agency priorities away from broad regulatory rulemaking towards targeted case-by-case enforcement, aligning with broader deregulatory trends and business interests.
4. All experts highlight that with less than three months until the question's resolution date, there is no viable legal, procedural, or political pathway for reviving and enacting the ban in its original or substantially similar form. Reviving a vacated and administratively abandoned federal rule in this time frame, especially under an opposing administration, is virtually unprecedented.
5. While the FTC may continue selective enforcement actions against egregious non-competes, this does not meet the resolution criteria of a nationwide, blanket ban 'in more or less its current form.'
6. No Congressional legislation or pending appeal could be identified that would alter this outcome before the deadline.

All forecasters agree that barring a highly improbable, dramatic reversal—whereby Congress or the courts would explicitly authorize and mandate quick enactment of a substantially unchanged rule—there is no path to a 'Yes' outcome by January 1, 2026. Forecasted probabilities range from 0% to 1%, with a clear consensus that the rule is 'dead' in the relevant timeframe.
